I cannot understand why she desired my friendship; yet, were the circumstances repeated, I am certain I should be deceived once more. Caroline returned my call only yesterday, and in all the interval I received neither a note nor a line. When she came, she plainly took no pleasure in the visit. She offered a brief, formal apology for not coming sooner, expressed no wish to see me again, and seemed so entirely changed that, by the time she left, I had firmly determined to pursue the acquaintance no further. I feel sorry for her, though I cannot avoid blaming her. She acted very wrongly in distinguishing me as she did; I can honestly declare that every step towards intimacy originated with her. Still, I pity her, because she must know her conduct has been wrong, and because I am convinced that concern for her brother explains it. I need not say more. Though we know that concern to be wholly unnecessary, if she feels it, it readily accounts for her treatment of me. Her brother is so deservedly dear to her that anxiety on his behalf must be natural and affectionate. I do wonder, however, that she retains such fears now; for if he had cared at all for me, we must surely have met long ago. Something she herself said assures me that he knows I am in town. Yet her manner of speaking suggested she was trying to convince herself of his attachment to Miss Darcy. I do not comprehend it. Were I less fearful of judging severely, I might almost say that the whole affair strongly resembles duplicity. I shall try to dismiss every distressing thought and dwell only upon what can give me happiness: your love, and the unfailing kindness of our dear aunt and uncle. Write very soon. Miss Bingley mentioned that he might never return to Netherfield and might give up the house, but spoke with no certainty. We had best say nothing of it. I am delighted by the pleasant reports you receive from our Hunsford friends. Do visit them with Sir William and Maria; I am sure you will find yourself very comfortable there.

“Yours, etc.”

Elizabeth felt some pain on reading this letter, but recovered her spirits when she considered that Jane would no longer be imposed upon, at least by the sister. Every hope concerning the brother had now entirely vanished.

At breakfast the following morning, the Otis family discussed the ghost at some length. Naturally, the United States Minister was slightly irritated that his gift had been refused. “I have no desire to injure the ghost,” he said, “and considering how long he has lived in this house, I must say that throwing pillows at him seems extremely impolite.” This perfectly reasonable observation, I regret to report, made the twins howl with laughter. “On the other hand,” he continued, “if he really refuses to use the Rising Sun Lubricator, we will have to confiscate his chains. Nobody can possibly sleep with that noise outside the bedrooms.”

The rest of the week passed without disturbance. Only the bloodstain’s constant reappearance on the library floor attracted attention. This was certainly strange, since Mr. Otis locked the door every night and the windows remained securely barred. The stain’s chameleon-like colors also caused considerable discussion. Some mornings it was a dull, almost Indian red; then it turned vermilion, then deep purple. Once, when the family came downstairs for prayers according to the simple ceremonies of the Free American Reformed Episcopalian Church, they found it bright emerald green. Naturally, these shifting colors amused everyone greatly, and they placed bets on the subject every evening. Only little Virginia declined to join in. For some unexplained reason, seeing the bloodstain always troubled her deeply. The morning it turned emerald green, she nearly cried.

The ghost appeared again on Sunday night. Shortly after the family went to bed, a tremendous crash in the hall startled them. They rushed downstairs and discovered that a large old suit of armor had come off its stand and fallen onto the stone floor. The Canterville ghost sat in a high-backed chair, rubbing his knees, his face expressing intense pain. The twins had brought their pea shooters and immediately fired two pellets at him. Their aim showed the precision achievable only through long, careful practice on a handwriting teacher. Meanwhile the United States Minister pointed his revolver at the ghost and, observing Californian etiquette, ordered him to put his hands up. With a furious shriek, the ghost sprang to his feet and swept through them like mist. As he passed, he put out Washington Otis’s candle, leaving everyone in complete darkness.

At last “Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” was brought to trial.

The judges wore feathered hats upon the Bench, though elsewhere the rough red cap with its tricoloured cockade predominated. Surveying the Jury and the unruly spectators, he might have fancied ordinary arrangements overturned, with criminals sitting in judgment upon honest men. The basest, most brutal, and most vicious inhabitants of a city always well supplied with baseness, brutality, and vice governed the proceedings. Unrestrained, they shouted comments, applauded, condemned, anticipated the verdict, and hurried it forward. Most men carried weapons of one kind or another. Some women wore knives, others daggers; some ate and drank while watching, and many knitted. One of the knitters worked with a spare piece tucked beneath her arm. She occupied the front row beside a man he had not seen since reaching the Barrier, but whom he instantly recognized as Defarge. Once or twice she whispered to him, and appeared to be his wife. What chiefly struck the prisoner, however, was that although the pair stood as near him as possible, neither glanced his way. With stubborn determination they seemed to await something, fixing their eyes upon the Jury and nowhere else. Doctor Manette sat below the President in his customary sober clothing. So far as the prisoner could distinguish, the Doctor and Mr. Lorry alone among men unconnected with the Tribunal had retained their ordinary dress instead of adopting the coarse Carmagnole.

The public prosecutor charged Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, with being an emigrant whose life belonged to the Republic under the decree excluding all emigrants on penalty of death. That the decree had been issued after his return to France counted for nothing. He was there; the decree was there. He had been captured in France, and his head was required.

“Off with his head!” the spectators shouted. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to still their voices, then asked whether the prisoner had indeed spent many years living in England.

It was certainly true.

Then was he not an emigrant? What did he consider himself?

Not an emigrant, he trusted, according to the law’s meaning and intention.

The President demanded to know why.

Because he had freely renounced both a title and a position he disliked, and left his native land—before, he submitted, the word emigrant had acquired its present meaning before the Tribunal—to support himself by his own labour in England instead of by the labour of France’s overburdened people.
